paragraphs.heading: Deep water rising
paragraphs.text: Upwelling is the wind-driven rise of deep ocean water to the surface. That deep water is dense, cool and usually full of nutrients, and it takes the place of warmer surface water that usually holds few nutrients. The extra nutrients help primary producers such as phytoplankton grow and multiply. Because of all that plankton and cool water, upwelling zones can be spotted by their cool sea surface temperatures and high levels of chlorophyll a.

paragraphs.heading: Wind, spin and a spiral
paragraphs.text: Three drivers act together to cause upwelling: wind, the Coriolis effect and Ekman transport. Wind blowing over the sea drags the top layer of water at about 45 degrees to its own direction, and friction with each layer below drags that one along too, setting up a spiral down through the water column. This pattern is Ekman transport, and its overall result is water moved at 90 degrees to the wind. The Coriolis effect sets the side: north of the equator the water goes to the right of the wind, and south of it to the left. Where this moving water spreads apart, deep water rises to fill the gap.

paragraphs.heading: Several kinds
paragraphs.text: Upwelling comes in at least five forms: along coasts, large-scale wind-driven upwelling in the open ocean, upwelling linked to eddies, upwelling tied to the shape of the seafloor, and broad, diffuse upwelling in the ocean interior. Coastal upwelling is the best known. It is also the type that touches people most, because it feeds some of the most productive fisheries on the planet.

paragraphs.heading: Fuel for the food chain
paragraphs.text: Deep water is rich in nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate and silicic acid, which come from dead plankton and other matter that sank from above and broke down. Once these reach the surface, phytoplankton combine them with dissolved CO₂ and sunlight to build organic compounds through photosynthesis. Upwelling regions therefore have far higher primary production, meaning the carbon fixed by phytoplankton, than other parts of the ocean, about 50% of the world's marine total. Since phytoplankton sit at the base of the ocean food chain, that wealth passes on up the chain.

paragraphs.heading: Big catches from small patches
paragraphs.text: More nutrients mean more primary production, and that in turn means more fish. About 25% of all marine fish caught worldwide come from just five upwellings, which together cover only 5% of the ocean. Upwellings driven by coastal currents or by open-ocean water spreading apart do the most to enrich the water and lift fishery yields.

paragraphs.heading: A green line at the equator
paragraphs.text: Upwelling at the equator goes with the Intertropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ, which shifts about and so often lies a little north or south of the equator. Trade winds from the northeast and southeast meet along the equator and blow west. There is no Coriolis force right on the equator, yet upwelling still happens just to its north and south. The water spreads apart there and nutrient-rich water wells up, so the equatorial Pacific shows up from space as a wide band of phytoplankton.
